headline: High-risk shared project-directory writes and broad shell/network access create default data-leakage and cascading-error exposure between gpt-engineer and ms-swift.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files in a shared project directory, so one agent’s generated content can be consumed by the other as trusted input. gpt-engineer explicitly “writes files then offers to run,” and ms-swift uses CLI/Python workflows over files and logs. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so this is not high, but the shared filesystem makes prompt injection plausible by default.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same project directory, file content from one can influence the other.
IF either agent parses repository files as instructions or prompts, injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Use separate project directories for each agent.
Add a manual review step before either agent reads files written by the other.
Prefix shared files with provenance labels.
Disable automatic execution of generated instructions.
requires-engineering: add filesystem namespace isolation or per-agent workspaces.

B_data_leakage.rationale: The pair shares a project directory and both have read/write filesystem access, so generated code, logs, configs, datasets, or checkpoints can flow between them. gpt-engineer touches generated source code and has broad network egress; ms-swift touches datasets, models, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files and can call external APIs. This is a default workspace leakage path, though not enough evidence for a higher severity.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same project directory, files written by one are readable by the other.
IF sensitive data is placed in logs, configs, checkpoints, or generated code, it can be exposed across the pair.
mitigations: Keep sensitive artifacts out of the shared project directory.
Separate logs, checkpoints, and source trees per agent.
Rotate or redact secrets before either agent writes files.
Restrict network access for the agent handling sensitive files.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write to the same project directory and can execute shells/spawn subprocesses. gpt-engineer explicitly supports per-project shared state, while ms-swift’s session scope is not stated, so there is no documented locking or coordination. Concurrent writes can overwrite code, configs, or outputs, and uncertainty about ms-swift’s coordination pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory concurrently, file clobbering can occur.
IF either agent modifies generated artifacts without locking, race conditions can corrupt outputs.
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time.
Assign separate output directories per agent.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
Review diffs before merging outputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer produces generated code and writes files, and ms-swift can consume files, logs, and configuration data in CLI/Python workflows. That creates a pathway where one agent’s output becomes the other’s input without a documented verification step. The pair does not show downstream email/commit authority, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF ms-swift ingests files produced by gpt-engineer without validation, errors can cascade.
IF gpt-engineer treats ms-swift outputs as authoritative prompts or code, mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a human verification step between agents.
Validate schemas and file formats before handoff.
Keep generated code and evaluation outputs in separate folders.
Require explicit provenance tags on handoff files.
requires-engineering: add automated contract checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files and calls third-party APIs such as ModelScope, HuggingFace, and OpenAI interfaces. gpt-engineer handles generated source code and broad network egress. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into ms-swift’s workflows, it can leave the local environment; the profiles do not prove a specific residency breach, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ms-swift datasets, logs, or checkpoints, external API calls may create a compliance issue.
IF gpt-engineer is used on sensitive source code while network egress is broad, policy review is required.
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in shared files.
Review API destinations before running ms-swift.
Use redacted or synthetic datasets.
Log data-class handling decisions for each run.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls per data class.
